title: Grow staple food
short: Containers, beds, soil, water, staple crops and seed saving
intro: A step-by-step learning track for growing food over months and years, starting with a few containers or a small bed and building toward storable staple crops and saved seed. Readings lean on University of California extension guides for coastal Southern California, with general manuals for the parts UC does not cover.

limits.text: Urban soil is often contaminated by past uses such as industry, dumping, traffic and lead paint; lead is especially risky for young children who may swallow soil.
UC Cooperative Extension does not test soil; the guide suggests using a soil lab and asking it questions before sampling.
Former industrial or manufacturing land and old gas station sites may need expert help to assess before growing food.
Fresh manure carries germs that cause illness; keep it away from waterways and wash hands and clothes after handling it.
Uncomposted manure can carry pathogens; the guide describes required waiting intervals between applying raw manure and harvest.
Signs of pesticide poisoning may appear right away or hours, days or years later; people may be exposed without knowing it.
Pesticides are more dangerous to children than adults; amounts that make adults sick may kill babies and children.
Sweet potatoes only crop well in warm areas and are injured by temperatures below 50°F; the guide is written for hotter Sacramento, not the coast.
Do not plant grocery store potatoes; use seed pieces certified free of pests and diseases.
